Senses.Note: Further collocations include “turn and shift step” (轉身移步), “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and “turn, then…” (轉身便). Later records use “turning phrase” (轉身句) as a label in stylized exchanges, while Zhongfeng criticizes stock phrases called by that name. Compare road to turn (轉身一路), turning phrase (轉身句), place to turn (轉身處), and shifting step (移步).

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: To turn oneself around is the bodily action of turning the body or self.
EvidenceBody: It is attested 2,135 times in 327 allowlisted texts. The action can be direct narration: Magu Baoche turns intending to sit and is struck, while Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang turns and immediately walks away. Chan records also build a productive family from the same turning action. Yuanwu Keqin defines a “place to turn oneself” by “speak at the place without words; go at the place where going cannot be done” (無言處言得，行不得處行得，謂之轉身處). Hongzhi Zhengjue says one must know a road to turn; Yinyuan Longqi directly asks what that road is and answers, “you travel in the wild grass; I again enter the deep village” (汝行荒草裏，我又入深村). An unnamed questioner asks Poshan Haiming “what is a turning phrase?” (如何是轉身句) and receives a recorded answer. Feiyin Tongrong says that bright-eyed patch-robed monks have “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and elsewhere pairs turning with shifting step. Literal motion and the road, place, and phrase compounds preserve one turning action; the former targets were paraphrases, not different referents.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The stored 轉身 witnesses show the corpus-specific deployment stated in the English opening and preserve its ordinary-language boundary.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: Further collocations include “turn and shift step” (轉身移步), “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and “turn, then…” (轉身便). Later records use “turning phrase” (轉身句) as a label in stylized exchanges, while Zhongfeng criticizes stock phrases called by that name. Compare road to turn (轉身一路), turning phrase (轉身句), place to turn (轉身處), and shifting step (移步).
